passages.section: Section 3a. A case is not a report
passages.text: Section 3a. A case is not a report. Two different things, and the agent produces both. **A case** (`CREATE_CASE`) is the bank's internal record of an investigation. Open one whenever fraud probability reaches 0.30, whenever you request evidence, or whenever a customer disputes a charge. A case can be closed as fraud or as legitimate. It can be updated when new evidence arrives. It should be written into the graph so later investigations can find it: a case that names a merchant or a device becomes evidence for the next analyst. **A suspicious activity report** (`FILE_REPORT`) is a regulatory filing sent outside the bank. File one when fraud is confirmed or strongly suspected **and** at least one of these holds: exposure exceeds $1,000; the activity connects to a shared device profile, a shared region cluster, or another customer's fraud; the pattern is coordinated or undocumented (rule R9). A report always has a case behind it. Most cases never need a report. The report narrative must stand on its own: who, what, when, where, how, and why it is suspicious. Deciding correctly between ""case only"" and ""case plus report"" is part of the next-best-action score.

assessment.reasoning: Transaction 3468463 ($144.21) on card C04274-K1 was flagged via graph monitoring because it used mobile device D004630, which belongs to fraud ring 57672119 and was marked as New to the account behind an anonymous proxy. While the bank's machine learning model gave the transaction a low score of 0.027 and a risk score of 0.11, the model only assesses single-transaction features and cannot observe cross-card graph linkages. Graph traversal reveals that device D004630 was utilized across 13 different cards within a 30-day window (with 12 other cards used concurrently between 2016-11-14 and 2016-11-18), appearing as a new device behind an anonymous proxy in every single instance. Furthermore, device D004630 is tied to four prior closed cases (CC-2649, CC-2971, CC-2985, and CC-3035), all of which were confirmed fraud where cardholders disputed unauthorized online purchases originating from this exact device profile. This coordinated exploitation across numerous customer accounts fits Rule R9 (undocumented pattern). The exculpatory signals—including the low model score, lack of a micro-authorization testing sequence, and baseline community lift of 0.0—are explained by the ring's modus operandi of conducting isolated moderate online purchases across distributed accounts to evade per-transaction detection thresholds. The overwhelming cross-card and device evidence confirms this transaction is part of an active multi-card fraud episode.

This repeated multi-card abuse has been confirmed as unauthorized across multiple prior cases but does not fit standard single-card fraud typologies.
